questions.q: Why does the editorial call the outlook “right here, right now” unworkable?
options: People cannot remember the present
Not quite. The article says: Human nature longs for the eternal, so a life planned for the present alone leaves a person under strain.
The present is always unpleasant
Not quite. The article says: Human nature longs for the eternal, so a life planned for the present alone leaves a person under strain.
Human nature longs for the eternal, so a life planned for the present alone leaves a person under strain
Yes. The post-death period must be taken into account.
Planning is impossible in modern life
Not quite. The article says: Human nature longs for the eternal, so a life planned for the present alone leaves a person under strain.
questions.rationale: “According to human nature, anything less than eternity cannot truly be man’s goal… The right attitude towards life is that which takes into account the post-death period.”

questions.q: To what does the article compare the troubles of this world?
options: A prison with no door
Not quite. The article says: A furnace that purifies ore – hardship forges a strong and shining personality.
A storm that destroys the harvest
Not quite. The article says: A furnace that purifies ore – hardship forges a strong and shining personality.
A debt that grows each year
Not quite. The article says: A furnace that purifies ore – hardship forges a strong and shining personality.
A furnace that purifies ore – hardship forges a strong and shining personality
Right. One must “learn to be happy without happiness.”
questions.rationale: “The troubles of the world act like the furnace required for the purification of ores… hardship and difficult experiences forge the personality of an individual.”

questions.q: When trouble comes, what does the article say the Quran asks a believer to do?
options: Look within for his own fault and correct it, not blame others
Yes. “Whatever misfortune befalls you is due to your own doing.”
Accept that nothing can be done
Not quite. The article says: Look within for his own fault and correct it, not blame others.
Identify who is responsible and oppose them
Not quite. The article says: Look within for his own fault and correct it, not blame others.
Wait for others to apologise
Not quite. The article says: Look within for his own fault and correct it, not blame others.
questions.rationale: “Whenever any trouble comes upon you, the only thing you must do is introspect to discover the fault within yourself which is the real cause of your troubles.”

questions.q: How does the Quran explain the Muslims’ setback at the Battle of Uhud, according to the article?
options: By bad weather on the day
Not quite. The article says: By their own failing – their courage failed and they disagreed among themselves.
By the greater numbers of the enemy
Not quite. The article says: By their own failing – their courage failed and they disagreed among themselves.
By betrayal from an ally
Not quite. The article says: By their own failing – their courage failed and they disagreed among themselves.
By their own failing – their courage failed and they disagreed among themselves
Well read. It does not dwell on the enemy’s plots.
questions.rationale: “‘…when your courage failed you and you disagreed among yourselves…’ (3:152). This verse is a clear lesson to the Muslims that they were not to lay the blame of their defeat in the battle on others.”

questions.q: What law of nature does the article draw from the form of the creed, a negation followed by an affirmation?
options: Something must be given up before something better can be gained
Correct. Truth cannot be held along with falsehood.
Every gain is followed by a loss
Not quite. The article says: Something must be given up before something better can be gained.
Habits form by themselves
Not quite. The article says: Something must be given up before something better can be gained.
Nothing can ever be given up
Not quite. The article says: Something must be given up before something better can be gained.
questions.rationale: “It is an abiding law of nature that only after relinquishing something will one be able to acquire something else.”

questions.q: The article compares a stuffed tiger in a museum with a live tiger in the jungle. What do they stand for?
options: Science and religion
Not quite. The article says: Inherited, lifeless belief in God, and conscious belief that stirs awe in the whole person.
Past greatness and present weakness
Not quite. The article says: Inherited, lifeless belief in God, and conscious belief that stirs awe in the whole person.
Inherited, lifeless belief in God, and conscious belief that stirs awe in the whole person
Yes. Where there is no awe, belief is only traditional.
Knowledge from books and from travel
Not quite. The article says: Inherited, lifeless belief in God, and conscious belief that stirs awe in the whole person.
questions.rationale: “A traditional belief in God is a lifeless belief… A conscious belief in God arises from discovering God and all His powers… his whole personality is shaken.”

questions.q: What does the article say of someone who readily says “O God, forgive me” but will not say “Brother, forgive me”?
options: That he should wait for the other to speak first
Not quite. The article says: That such reluctance goes against the spirit of faith.
That such reluctance goes against the spirit of faith
Right. “Sorry, I was wrong” restores relations at once.
That forgiveness from people is not needed
Not quite. The article says: That such reluctance goes against the spirit of faith.
That he is right to keep the two apart
Not quite. The article says: That such reluctance goes against the spirit of faith.
questions.rationale: “A true man of faith will say to another: ‘Forgive me,’ just as easily as he says to God: ‘O Lord, forgive me.’”

questions.q: The chemicals in a human body are worth only a few dollars. What does the article ask us to see in this?
options: That science can now make a human being
Not quite. The article says: The wonder that God has made a living, thinking being, beyond price, from matter of no value.
The wonder that God has made a living, thinking being, beyond price, from matter of no value
Yes. People marvel at a conjurer but not at this.
That the body matters less than money
Not quite. The article says: The wonder that God has made a living, thinking being, beyond price, from matter of no value.
That human life is cheap
Not quite. The article says: The wonder that God has made a living, thinking being, beyond price, from matter of no value.
questions.rationale: “Out of this four hundred rupees worth of matter, God has created a human being so wonderful that no price can be set upon him.”

questions.q: Why, according to the article, does the Quran link gratitude with patience?
options: Life is full of hardship, and only one who bears it patiently can remain thankful
Exactly. Patience also keeps the mind clear to respond wisely.
Because gratitude is owed only after long waiting
Not quite. The article says: Life is full of hardship, and only one who bears it patiently can remain thankful.
Because the two words sound alike in Arabic
Not quite. The article says: Life is full of hardship, and only one who bears it patiently can remain thankful.
Because the patient receive more than others
Not quite. The article says: Life is full of hardship, and only one who bears it patiently can remain thankful.
questions.rationale: “It is only when a man patiently endures worldly problems that it is possible for him to express his feeling of gratefulness to God.”

questions.q: A paratrooper climbed along the outside of a speeding train to reach the guard and save a fallen comrade. What does the article take from his act?
options: Courage is a matter of training alone
Not quite. The article says: Success comes to one who forgets himself in single-minded pursuit of the goal.
Rules should always be followed first
Not quite. The article says: Success comes to one who forgets himself in single-minded pursuit of the goal.
Trains ought to be made safer
Not quite. The article says: Success comes to one who forgets himself in single-minded pursuit of the goal.
Success comes to one who forgets himself in single-minded pursuit of the goal
Well read. He thought only of the fallen soldier.
questions.rationale: “To succeed in life, one must do what Kailash Chand did. One should put aside all thoughts about oneself and relentlessly pursue one’s goal.”
